items.stem: Which UN Secretary-General’s An Agenda for Peace (1992) defined preventive diplomacy, peacemaking, peacekeeping and post-conflict peacebuilding?
items.answer: Boutros Boutros-Ghali
items.markingKey: B. The report followed the end of the Cold War and a surge in UN operations.

items.stem: Explain why UN peacekeeping missions have sometimes lost local legitimacy.
items.answer: Failures to protect civilians, sexual exploitation and abuse by some peacekeepers, the introduction of cholera to Haiti in 2010, and close association with unpopular governments have eroded trust, as with MINUSMA in Mali and MONUSCO in the DRC.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Failures to protect civilians, sexual exploitation and abuse by some peacekeepers, the introduction of cholera to Haiti in 2010, and close association with unpopular governments have eroded trust, as with MINUSMA in Mali and MONUSCO in the DRC. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between peacekeeping and peacebuilding.
items.answer: Peacekeeping maintains security and monitors ceasefires once fighting has stopped; peacebuilding is the longer-term transformation of institutions, economies and relationships to prevent relapse.
items.markingKey: Peacekeeping maintains security and monitors ceasefires once fighting has stopped; peacebuilding is the longer-term transformation of institutions, economies and relationships to prevent relapse. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Peacekeeping only involves soldiers monitoring ceasefire lines." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Modern multidimensional missions include police, civilian staff, electoral assistance, human rights monitoring and support for justice systems.
items.markingKey: Modern multidimensional missions include police, civilian staff, electoral assistance, human rights monitoring and support for justice systems. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe the UN mission in Sierra Leone (UNAMSIL, 1999–2005) and explain what it reveals about successful peacekeeping and peacebuilding.
items.answer: After initial failure and the RUF’s seizure of 500 peacekeepers in 2000, a reinforced mission (and British intervention) disarmed about 75,000 combatants and supported elections in 2002. A robust, well-resourced mission combined security with disarmament and elections, contributing to lasting peace.
items.markingKey: Context (After initial failure and the RUF’s seizure of 500 peacekeepers in 2000, a reinforced mission (and British intervention) disarmed about 75,000 combatants and supported elections in 2002.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A robust, well-resourced mission combined security with disarmament and elections, contributing to lasting peace. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to successful peacekeeping and peacebuilding.

items.stem:
Source B
The United Nations does not wage war. Where enforcement action is required, it has consistently been entrusted to coalitions of willing states. But once deployed, peacekeepers must be able to carry out their mandates professionally and successfully, including defending themselves and other mission components.
— Report of the Panel on United Nations Peace Operations (the Brahimi Report), 2000 (paraphrased)

Using evidence from Source B, explain how the source reflects lessons learned from failures such as Srebrenica. [4]
items.answer: By insisting that peacekeepers must be able to defend themselves and their mandate, the report responds to cases where weak, under-resourced missions watched atrocities occur; it calls for credible capability while leaving enforcement to coalitions.
items.markingKey: By insisting that peacekeepers must be able to defend themselves and their mandate, the report responds to cases where weak, under-resourced missions watched atrocities occur; it calls for credible capability while leaving enforcement to coalitions. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "UN peacekeeping has been more successful than its critics claim."
items.answer: Peacekeeping has a better record than its high-profile failures suggest, though its effectiveness depends on mandates, resources and consent.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: research shows peacekeeping reduces civilian killings and relapse (e.g. Fortna, Hultman); successes in Sierra Leone, Liberia, Timor-Leste; cheaper than unilateral intervention. Arguments against: failures in Rwanda, Srebrenica and the DRC; scandals of sexual abuse and cholera in Haiti; expulsions from Mali (2023) and drawdown in the DRC. Supported judgement: Peacekeeping has a better record than its high-profile failures suggest, though its effectiveness depends on mandates, resources and consent.

items.stem: Briefly explain why peacebuilding is necessary after a peace agreement.
items.answer: About half of post-conflict countries have historically relapsed into conflict within a decade; peacebuilding addresses root causes – weak institutions, exclusion, unemployment of ex-combatants – that a ceasefire alone leaves untouched.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The processes and mechanisms – prosecutions, truth commissions, reparations, institutional reform – used by societies to deal with legacies of large-scale abuses"?
items.answer: transitional justice
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of transitional justice.

items.stem: Distinguish between retributive justice and restorative justice.
items.answer: Retributive justice punishes perpetrators through prosecution; restorative justice seeks to repair harm and rebuild relationships through truth-telling, apology and reparations.
items.markingKey: Retributive justice punishes perpetrators through prosecution; restorative justice seeks to repair harm and rebuild relationships through truth-telling, apology and reparations. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why South Africa chose a truth commission rather than mass prosecutions.
items.answer: The negotiated transition required compromise with the outgoing regime and security forces; amnesty in exchange for truth encouraged disclosure, prioritised reconciliation and nation-building, and avoided overwhelming the courts. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The negotiated transition required compromise with the outgoing regime and security forces; amnesty in exchange for truth encouraged disclosure, prioritised reconciliation and nation-building, and avoided overwhelming the courts. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Source C
Retributive justice is largely Western. The African understanding is far more restorative – not so much to punish as to redress or restore a balance that has been knocked askew. Ubuntu says I am human because I belong.
— Archbishop Desmond Tutu, No Future Without Forgiveness (1999) (paraphrased)

Using evidence from Source C, explain how the source justifies the approach taken by South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission. [3]
items.answer: Tutu presents restorative justice, rooted in ubuntu, as culturally appropriate: restoring relationships and balance rather than punishing, which justifies truth-telling and conditional amnesty over mass prosecutions.

items.stem:
Source B
Impunity for the worst crimes undermines any peace. Those who commit genocide and crimes against humanity must face justice, or victims will take revenge and future leaders will believe they can act without consequences.
— Statement by the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court (2015) (paraphrased)

Outline three points made in Source B about transitional justice. [3]
items.answer: impunity undermines peace; without justice victims may take revenge; future leaders would believe they can act without consequences (deterrence)
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to [3]: impunity undermines peace; without justice victims may take revenge; future leaders would believe they can act without consequences (deterrence). items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "International criminal justice is selective and politically biased."
items.answer: Selectivity is real because of jurisdiction and power, but recent cases show the system is broadening.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: most early ICC cases concerned African states; major powers are outside its jurisdiction; Security Council referrals depend on great-power politics. Arguments against: the ICC issued warrants for Vladimir Putin (2023) and Israeli and Hamas leaders (2024); many African cases were self-referrals; ad hoc tribunals convicted leaders from several regions. Supported judgement: Selectivity is real because of jurisdiction and power, but recent cases show the system is broadening.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "retributive justice".
items.answer: An approach focusing on punishing perpetrators in proportion to their crimes, as in international tribunals
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an approach focusing on punishing perpetrators in proportion to their crimes, as in international tribunals. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly describe South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission (1996–1998) and explain what it reveals about restorative transitional justice.
items.answer: About 21,000 victims gave statements; over 7,000 people applied for amnesty, of whom only a minority received it, because amnesty required full disclosure of politically motivated crimes. Public testimony acknowledged victims and created a shared record, but many victims felt reparations and prosecutions were inadequate.
items.markingKey: Context (About 21,000 victims gave statements; over 7,000 people applied for amnesty, of whom only a minority received it, because amnesty required full disclosure of politically motivated crimes.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.answer: Peace and justice can conflict in the short term, but sustainable peace usually requires some form of justice.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: ICC warrants and peace negotiations (Uganda, Sudan); amnesty in South Africa; deterrence of future crimes; sequencing justice after peace. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "reintegration"?
options: An approach focusing on punishing perpetrators in proportion to their crimes, as in international tribunals
An official, temporary body that investigates a pattern of past abuses and produces a report, such as South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission (1996–1998)
The process by which ex-combatants acquire civilian status and gain sustainable employment and income, which is social, economic and political
An approach focusing on repairing harm and restoring relationships between victims, perpetrators and communities, rather than punishment
items.answer: The process by which ex-combatants acquire civilian status and gain sustainable employment and income, which is social, economic and political
items.markingKey: C. "reintegration" is the process by which ex-combatants acquire civilian status and gain sustainable employment and income, which is social, economic and political.

items.stem: Explain why reintegration is often the most difficult stage of DDR.
items.answer: Ex-combatants need jobs, land and acceptance in communities that may fear or resent them; weak post-war economies offer few opportunities, and without livelihoods former fighters may rejoin armed groups or crime.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Ex-combatants need jobs, land and acceptance in communities that may fear or resent them; weak post-war economies offer few opportunities, and without livelihoods former fighters may rejoin armed groups or crime. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Post-conflict reconstruction is only about rebuilding roads and buildings." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Reconstruction also involves rebuilding institutions, the economy, the security sector and social trust.
items.markingKey: Reconstruction also involves rebuilding institutions, the economy, the security sector and social trust. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source B
Reintegration is not a short-term event but a long-term process. Former combatants must find a place in communities that have suffered, and those communities must see that peace brings benefits for them, not only for those who carried guns.
— United Nations, Integrated Disarmament, Demobilization and Reintegration Standards (revised 2019) (paraphrased)

With reference to Source B, explain why the source suggests that DDR should be community-based. [3]
items.answer: If only ex-combatants benefit, communities may resent them and reintegration fails; community-based programmes share benefits, rebuild trust and make peace a collective gain.
items.markingKey: If only ex-combatants benefit, communities may resent them and reintegration fails; community-based programmes share benefits, rebuild trust and make peace a collective gain. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why DDR programmes need to address women and child soldiers specifically.
items.answer: Women associated with armed groups (as fighters, cooks or forced “wives”) and children are often excluded from programmes designed for male fighters, leaving them without support and facing stigma.

items.stem: With reference to post-genocide reconstruction in Rwanda, explain how it illustrates the relationship between reconstruction and political freedom.
items.answer: Under the RPF government Rwanda achieved rapid growth (often 7–8 per cent a year) and improved health indicators, while restricting political opposition and media. Rwanda shows that state-led reconstruction can produce development and stability, but at the cost of political pluralism.
items.markingKey: Context (Under the RPF government Rwanda achieved rapid growth (often 7–8 per cent a year) and improved health indicators, while restricting political opposition and media.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The model of peacebuilding that promotes democracy, market economics, human rights and the rule of law as the basis of peace after conflict"?
items.answer: liberal peace
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of liberal peace.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the liberal peace and a hybrid peace.
items.answer: The liberal peace is an externally promoted template of democracy, markets and rule of law; a hybrid peace combines international norms with local institutions and practices that shape how peace works.
items.markingKey: The liberal peace is an externally promoted template of democracy, markets and rule of law; a hybrid peace combines international norms with local institutions and practices that shape how peace works. items.stem: Elena writes: "Local ownership means international actors should withdraw completely." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It means international actors support processes led by local people; resources and guarantees from outside may still be essential.
items.markingKey: It means international actors support processes led by local people; resources and guarantees from outside may still be essential. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to state-building in Afghanistan (2001–2021), explain how it illustrates the limits of the liberal peace.
items.answer: International actors spent over $140 billion on reconstruction and created a centralised democratic state; it collapsed when the Taliban took Kabul in August 2021. An externally designed, aid-dependent state lacked legitimacy and capacity, illustrating critics’ arguments about imposed models.
items.markingKey: Context (International actors spent over $140 billion on reconstruction and created a centralised democratic state; it collapsed when the Taliban took Kabul in August 2021.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: An externally designed, aid-dependent state lacked legitimacy and capacity, illustrating critics’ arguments about imposed models. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the limits of the liberal peace.

Using evidence from Source C, explain how the source critiques the liberal peace while accepting its goals. [4]
items.answer: Paris accepts democracy and markets as goals but argues that introducing them too early destabilises fragile societies; he recommends sequencing, with institution-building first.

items.stem: Briefly explain why local ownership is difficult to achieve in practice.
items.answer: Donors control funds and set priorities, local elites may capture processes, and there are competing “locals”; international timetables often prioritise quick, measurable results over slow local processes.

items.stem: "The liberal peace model has failed in post-conflict societies." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: The liberal peace has a mixed record; it fails when imposed rapidly without local legitimacy and institutions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Afghanistan’s collapse in 2021; South Sudan relapsed in 2013; elections polarised Bosnia along ethnic lines. Arguments against: democratic peace in Sierra Leone, Liberia and Timor-Leste; liberal values are widely demanded by local populations; failures often reflect implementation, not the model. items.stem: With reference to DDR in Colombia after the 2016 peace agreement, explain how it illustrates political reintegration of former combatants.

items.stem: Evaluate the effectiveness of UN peace operations in maintaining peace after civil wars. [15]
items.answer: UN operations are effective when consent, robust mandates and resources align, but fail when they are asked to keep a peace that does not exist.

items.stem: "Truth commissions are more effective than criminal trials in promoting reconciliation after conflict." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Truth commissions support acknowledgement and reconciliation, but they are most effective alongside some prosecutions and reparations.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: South Africa’s TRC created a shared record and avoided civil war; trials focus on few perpetrators; victims are heard publicly. Arguments against: many victims felt betrayed by amnesty and limited reparations; trials (ICTY, Taylor) establish accountability and deter; reconciliation may need both (Sierra Leone had both a TRC and a Special Court). Supported judgement: Truth commissions support acknowledgement and reconciliation, but they are most effective alongside some prosecutions and reparations. items.stem: "DDR programmes are essential but rarely sufficient to secure lasting peace." Discuss.
items.answer: DDR is a necessary component of peacebuilding, but it succeeds only within credible political agreements and economic recovery.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Sierra Leone’s DDR contributed to durable peace; reduces weapons and armed groups; gives ex-combatants an alternative. Arguments against: Liberia and Colombia show implementation problems; peace depends on political settlement and security sector reform; economic opportunities determine reintegration. Supported judgement: DDR is a necessary component of peacebuilding, but it succeeds only within credible political agreements and economic recovery. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Brahimi Report"?
options: An official, temporary body that investigates a pattern of past abuses and produces a report, such as South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission (1996–1998)
The 2000 Report of the Panel on United Nations Peace Operations, which called for robust mandates, adequate resources and realistic, achievable goals
UN operations that combine military tasks with civilian functions such as elections, policing, the rule of law and human rights, as in MONUSCO or UNMISS
The principle that people in post-conflict societies should lead and control peacebuilding processes

items.markingKey: C. The UN verified the handover of about 8,000 weapons by mid-2017.

items.stem: Explain why critics argue that the liberal peace can destabilise post-conflict societies.
items.answer: Rapid elections can polarise societies along conflict lines and reward warlords, and fast market liberalisation can increase inequality; Roland Paris pointed to Angola (1992) and Rwanda (1990s) where early liberalisation preceded renewed violence.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Rapid elections can polarise societies along conflict lines and reward warlords, and fast market liberalisation can increase inequality; Roland Paris pointed to Angola (1992) and Rwanda (1990s) where early liberalisation preceded renewed violence. items.stem: Explain the difference between peacebuilding and peacekeeping.
items.answer: Peacekeeping maintains security and monitors ceasefires once fighting has stopped; peacebuilding is the longer-term transformation of institutions, economies and relationships to prevent relapse.
items.markingKey: Peacekeeping maintains security and monitors ceasefires once fighting has stopped; peacebuilding is the longer-term transformation of institutions, economies and relationships to prevent relapse. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between the ICC and ad hoc tribunals such as the ICTY and ICTR.
items.answer: The ICC is a permanent court based on a treaty (the Rome Statute) with jurisdiction over crimes since 2002; ad hoc tribunals were created by the UN Security Council for specific conflicts and time periods.
items.markingKey: The ICC is a permanent court based on a treaty (the Rome Statute) with jurisdiction over crimes since 2002; ad hoc tribunals were created by the UN Security Council for specific conflicts and time periods. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between reintegration and disarmament.
items.answer: Disarmament removes weapons from combatants in the short term; reintegration is the long-term social and economic process of returning former fighters to civilian life.
items.markingKey: Disarmament removes weapons from combatants in the short term; reintegration is the long-term social and economic process of returning former fighters to civilian life. items.stem: Distinguish between the liberal peace and a hybrid peace.
items.answer: The liberal peace is an externally promoted template of democracy, markets and rule of law; a hybrid peace combines international norms with local institutions and practices that shape how peace works.
items.markingKey: The liberal peace is an externally promoted template of democracy, markets and rule of law; a hybrid peace combines international norms with local institutions and practices that shape how peace works. items.stem: Explain why robust peacekeeping mandates are controversial.
items.answer: Authorising peacekeepers to use force to protect civilians (e.g. the Force Intervention Brigade in the DRC, 2013) can save lives but compromises impartiality, makes peacekeepers parties to the conflict and endangers troops.

items.stem: Briefly describe state-building in Afghanistan (2001–2021) and explain what it reveals about the limits of the liberal peace.
items.answer: International actors spent over $140 billion on reconstruction and created a centralised democratic state; it collapsed when the Taliban took Kabul in August 2021. An externally designed, aid-dependent state lacked legitimacy and capacity, illustrating critics’ arguments about imposed models.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Somaliland since 1991 shows locally owned peacebuilding.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "UN peacekeeping has been more successful than its critics claim."
items.answer: Peacekeeping has a better record than its high-profile failures suggest, though its effectiveness depends on mandates, resources and consent.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: research shows peacekeeping reduces civilian killings and relapse (e.g. Fortna, Hultman); successes in Sierra Leone, Liberia, Timor-Leste; cheaper than unilateral intervention. Arguments against: failures in Rwanda, Srebrenica and the DRC; scandals of sexual abuse and cholera in Haiti; expulsions from Mali (2023) and drawdown in the DRC. Supported judgement: Peacekeeping has a better record than its high-profile failures suggest, though its effectiveness depends on mandates, resources and consent.

items.stem: Examine the view that international criminal justice is selective and politically biased. Use relevant key concepts and named examples in your answer. [15]
items.answer: Selectivity is real because of jurisdiction and power, but recent cases show the system is broadening.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: most early ICC cases concerned African states; major powers are outside its jurisdiction; Security Council referrals depend on great-power politics. Possible judgement: Selectivity is real because of jurisdiction and power, but recent cases show the system is broadening. items.stem: "The liberal peace model has failed in post-conflict societies." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: The liberal peace has a mixed record; it fails when imposed rapidly without local legitimacy and institutions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Afghanistan’s collapse in 2021; South Sudan relapsed in 2013; elections polarised Bosnia along ethnic lines.
